title: Week 10 · Lesson 28: Pain Pathophysiology — FNP-Level Approach
html:
PHASE 1 · ADVANCED PATHOPHYSIOLOGY + CLINICAL REASONING

Week 10 — Lesson 28: Pain Pathophysiology

FNP-level goal: Explain acute, inflammatory, nociceptive, neuropathic, and chronic pain mechanisms; identify dangerous pain presentations; build a functional and biopsychosocial assessment; and use safe, multimodal treatment and referral reasoning.

Learning Objectives

  • Trace nociception from peripheral transduction to conscious pain perception.
  • Differentiate nociceptive, neuropathic, nociplastic/central-sensitization, visceral, and referred pain patterns.
  • Recognize red flags requiring emergency evaluation rather than routine pain management.
  • Assess function, safety, substance-use risk, and patient goals in chronic pain.
  • Apply multimodal, patient-centered, nonopioid-first pain-management principles.

Part 1 — Pain Is a Protective Signal, Not Just a Number

Pain begins when noxious mechanical, thermal, inflammatory, or chemical stimuli activate nociceptors. The signal travels through peripheral nerves to the spinal cord and brain, where it is interpreted in the context of attention, emotion, prior experience, sleep, threat, and social environment.

Nociception is neural encoding of harmful stimuli. Pain is the conscious experience. The two are related but not identical: severe pain may occur without visible tissue injury, and serious injury may present with surprisingly little pain in neuropathy or altered sensation.

Part 2 — The Nociceptive Pathway

Peripheral injury releases mediators such as prostaglandins, bradykinin, cytokines, hydrogen ions, and substance P. These lower nociceptor thresholds and produce peripheral sensitization. Signals enter the dorsal horn, ascend through spinal pathways, and are modulated by descending inhibitory and facilitatory circuits.

Tissue injury/inflammation → nociceptor activation → spinal transmission → brain interpretation → protective behavior. This framework explains why anti-inflammatory strategies may help inflammatory pain but are not a complete answer for neuropathic or centrally amplified pain.

Part 3 — Nociceptive and Inflammatory Pain

Nociceptive pain results from actual or threatened tissue injury. Somatic pain from skin, muscle, bone, or joint is often localized and aching/sharp. Visceral pain from internal organs can be diffuse, cramping, poorly localized, and associated with autonomic symptoms. Inflammatory pain may produce warmth, swelling, stiffness, and pain with movement, as in arthritis or tissue injury.

Do not let a familiar musculoskeletal label hide dangerous alternatives: fracture, septic arthritis, compartment syndrome, ischemia, DVT, malignancy, spinal infection, and referred visceral pain may mimic routine strain.

Part 4 — Neuropathic Pain

Neuropathic pain arises from lesion or disease of the somatosensory nervous system. Patients may describe burning, electric shocks, shooting pain, tingling, numbness, pins-and-needles, or pain from normally nonpainful touch (allodynia). Examples include diabetic peripheral neuropathy, radiculopathy, postherpetic neuralgia, chemotherapy-related neuropathy, and entrapment neuropathy.

Neurologic examination matters: sensory distribution, strength, reflexes, gait, autonomic symptoms, skin integrity, and focal deficits can identify localization and urgency. New weakness, saddle anesthesia, bladder/bowel dysfunction, rapidly progressive deficit, or myelopathic findings need emergency assessment.

Part 5 — Central Sensitization and Chronic Pain

Persistent nociceptive input can change peripheral and central processing. Peripheral sensitization lowers activation thresholds near injured tissue. Central sensitization amplifies responsiveness within the spinal cord and brain; normal input can become painful and pain can spread beyond the original site.

Chronic pain is not evidence that symptoms are imagined. It is a biopsychosocial condition in which sleep disruption, mood disorders, trauma, deconditioning, fear avoidance, isolation, and ongoing nociceptive disease may sustain disability. Treat the patient’s function and quality of life, not only a numeric pain score.

Part 6 — Acute, Subacute, and Chronic Time Frames

Acute pain generally lasts less than one month and often reflects injury, surgery, or acute illness. Subacute pain persists roughly one to three months. Chronic pain persists beyond expected healing, commonly beyond three months, and requires reassessment of diagnosis, function, contributing mechanisms, mental health, sleep, and treatment harms.

A changing pattern is a warning. New focal neurologic findings, systemic symptoms, progressive night pain, unexplained weight loss, fever, immunosuppression, cancer history, trauma, or rapidly worsening function should prompt a new diagnostic pathway rather than automatic escalation of analgesics.

Part 7 — Pain Red Flags and Emergency Disposition

Emergency evaluation is appropriate for suspected acute coronary syndrome, aortic syndrome, pulmonary embolism, acute limb ischemia, compartment syndrome, cauda equina syndrome, spinal epidural infection/compression, septic arthritis, acute abdomen, ectopic pregnancy, testicular torsion, severe infection/sepsis, or uncontrolled pain with instability.

Examples include chest pressure with dyspnea/diaphoresis; severe back pain plus fever or neurologic deficits; pain out of proportion with pallor/pulselessness; a hot swollen joint with fever; sudden unilateral testicular/pelvic pain; or severe headache with neurologic deficit. Do not convert a potentially time-sensitive diagnosis into a “chronic pain visit.”

Part 8 — FNP Assessment

Ask location, onset, trigger, timing, quality, severity, radiation, aggravating/relieving factors, associated symptoms, functional impact, sleep, mood, work, mobility, trauma, cancer/infection history, medications, substances, and prior treatments. Examine the relevant system plus neurologic, vascular, skin, gait, and mental-status domains as indicated.

Use tests purposefully. Imaging and laboratory studies should answer a diagnostic question, not substitute for a history/examination. Document baseline function and collaboratively select a measurable goal: walking, sleeping, working, caring for family, or returning to valued activity.

Part 9 — Multimodal Pain Management

Multimodal care may include treatment of the underlying disorder, movement/exercise or physical therapy, sleep optimization, behavioral therapies, coping skills, weight management where relevant, topical or systemic nonopioid medications, interventional or specialty referral, and careful follow-up. The appropriate plan depends on pain mechanism, comorbidity, risk, and patient goals.

Nonopioid and nonpharmacologic therapies are preferred for subacute and chronic pain. If opioid therapy is considered, it requires an individualized benefit-risk discussion, the lowest effective exposure consistent with current guidance, avoidance of dangerous combinations, monitoring, and a plan for reassessment; do not abruptly discontinue established therapy without a patient-centered clinical plan.

Part 10 — FNP Clinical Reasoning Case 1

A 59-year-old with diabetes reports burning bilateral foot pain, numbness, reduced vibration sense, and allodynia. Mechanism: peripheral neuropathic pain. FNP approach: assess glycemic context, feet/skin, gait/fall risk, alternate causes, function, sleep, and safe mechanism-targeted management.

Part 11 — FNP Clinical Reasoning Case 2

A 47-year-old with chronic low back pain now has fever, severe night pain, new urinary retention, and progressive leg weakness. FNP decision: this is not routine back-pain follow-up; assess urgently for spinal infection/compression or cauda equina syndrome and arrange emergency evaluation.

Part 12 — FNP Clinical Reasoning Case 3

A patient with persistent widespread pain sleeps poorly, avoids activity because of pain flares, has depressed mood, and reports loss of function. FNP approach: validate the experience, identify pain mechanisms and comorbidities, set functional goals, address sleep/mood/movement, and avoid the false choice between “all physical” and “all psychological.”

FNP High-Yield Framework

Nociceptive: tissue injury/inflammation; often localized or visceral.
Neuropathic: lesion/disease of somatosensory system; burning, electric, allodynia, numbness.
Central sensitization: amplified pain processing; real pain may outlast tissue healing.
Chronic pain care: function + safety + multimodal plan + reassessment.
Never miss: ischemia, infection, neurologic compression, acute abdomen/pelvic/testicular emergency, major trauma, cancer-related warning patterns, and life-threatening chest/head pain.
